## Flags on every command

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--url <url>` | Kantel's URL (KANTEL_URL; default https://app.kantel.dev) |
| `--key <key>` | A personal access token or API key (KANTEL_API_KEY); also --api-key |
| `--account <id\|name>` | The account to act in, by ID or name (KANTEL_ACCOUNT); default the one kantel org use saved |
| `--json` | Print Kantel's JSON answer as it is |
| `-h, --help` | Show a command's help |

## Exit codes

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | it worked |
| 1 | it failed: the error's code says why |
| 2 | it was used wrongly, and did nothing |
| 4 | it needs a credential that works: kantel login, or KANTEL_API_KEY |

With --json a failure is the last line on stderr, as JSON: {"error": {"code", "message", "hint"?, "exitCode", …}}.

## Signing in

### kantel login

Sign in in the browser, or with a token or API key, and save it for the commands after.

```sh
kantel login [flags]
```

With no key it prints a code and opens Kantel's console, where you approve it; the CLI gets a personal access token of its own (90 days), which acts as you in every account you belong to: --account, or kantel org use, picks the one a command acts in. You can revoke it with kantel token revoke, or under Profile in the console. --account-key asks for an API key in one account instead, which needs admin there. With no terminal it prints the URL and code and exits; run kantel login --wait to wait for the approval. Running it again shows the same code. It signs in to https://app.kantel.dev unless you give --url (or KANTEL_URL), for a self-hosted Kantel.

An existing key comes from --key-stdin, which keeps it out of your shell history and process list:

```sh
printf %s "$KANTEL_API_KEY" | kantel login --key-stdin --url https://kantel.example
```

It is saved, readable by you only, in ~/.config/kantel/config.json (or under XDG_CONFIG_HOME).

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--key-stdin` | Read a personal access token or API key from stdin rather than signing in in the browser |
| `--account-key` | Ask for an API key in one account (picked in the browser) rather than a personal token |
| `--no-browser` | Print the sign-in URL but don't open it |
| `--wait` | Wait for the browser sign-in even with no terminal (agents, scripts) |
| `--name <name>` | The new token's name (default kantel on &lt;host&gt;) |

```sh
# Sign in in the browser, to the hosted Kantel
kantel login

# Sign in to your own Kantel
kantel login --url https://kantel.example.com

# Save a token or key you have, kept out of your shell history
printf %s "$KANTEL_API_KEY" | kantel login --key-stdin
```

### kantel logout

Forget the saved token or API key, revoking a personal token.

```sh
kantel logout [flags]
```

### kantel whoami

Who you are signed in as, and the accounts you may act in.

```sh
kantel whoami [flags]
```

## Sandboxes

### kantel new

Create a sandbox and wait until it runs.

```sh
kantel new [flags]
```

Also: `kantel create`, `kantel sandbox create`, `kantel sandbox new`.

--auto-upgrade makes an isolate upgrade itself to a microVM (as kantel upgrade does) when a command needs something an isolate doesn't have (a program such as tar, a package manager, Docker), and run that command again there, once. Without it the command says it needs a microVM, and the isolate stays one.

--env takes a variable (K=V) or an environment (its name or env_… ID; kantel env list shows them). An environment gives the sandbox its variables, secret files, repos and grants: a protected variable arrives as a kph_… placeholder that the egress proxy swaps for the value only where it is bound.

Give --env &lt;env&gt; more than once for several environments, in order (up to 10): where two set the same variable, secret file or repo path, the later one wins, and the K=V variables win over them all. Their grants add up. kantel env attach and kantel env detach change a sandbox's environments later.

--disk sizes a microVM's disk apart from its vCPUs and memory (kantel new --type microvm --size large --disk 60). A sandbox made from a snapshot keeps the snapshot's disk.

--size takes one of the named sizes the hosts offer; kantel sizes lists them, and the most --vcpus and --memory may ask for. --vcpus and --memory size a microVM beyond the named sizes (kantel new --type microvm --vcpus 8 --memory 16), within what a host offers. A large monorepo's type-check needs about 16 GB, and its tests about 32.

--from with --size, or --vcpus and --memory, starts a snapshot of the disk alone (the default for kantel snapshot save) on that machine: kantel new --from monorepo-ci --vcpus 8 --memory 16. A snapshot that holds its sandbox's memory (saved with --memory) has that sandbox's machine, and Kantel refuses another. Without them, a sandbox from a snapshot is the machine the snapshot was taken of.

--idle-stop stops it once nobody has used it for that long, beside --auto-stop's lifetime: with --auto-stop never --idle-stop 30 it runs while people use it, and stops 30 minutes after they stop. Its disk is kept; kantel resume starts it again. A request to a hosted port of a stopped sandbox gets a page saying it is stopped and why: it doesn't wake it.

--on puts it on one host: one of the account's own hosts, or for a super-admin any host. It stays there, as every sandbox stays on the host it was placed on. Without it, Kantel picks the host.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--type <isolate\|microvm>` | isolate (default): starts in milliseconds; microvm: a full Linux with Docker and SSH |
| `--size <size>` | A microVM's named size, such as small, default or large (kantel sizes lists the hosts') |
| `--disk <GB>` | A microVM's disk in GB, whatever its size (default: its size's); within the hosts' limits |
| `--vcpus <n>` | A microVM's vCPUs, in place of --size; with --memory |
| `--memory <GB>` | A microVM's memory in GB, in place of --size; with --vcpus |
| `--name <name>` | Default: a generated name |
| `--from <snapshot>` | Start from a snapshot's ID or a saved one's name |
| `--image <image>` | A microVM's base image |
| `--auto-stop <minutes\|never>` | Stop by itself this long after it starts (default 60) |
| `--idle-stop <minutes\|never>` | Also stop once it goes this long unused: no command, SSH, desktop, browser or port traffic (default never) |
| `--label <k=v>` | A label; repeat for more |
| `-e, --env <K=V\|env>` | K=V: a variable every command sees (not a secret); or an environment to start from. Repeat it for more |
| `--host <port[:public]>` | Give this port an HTTPS URL once it runs; repeat it |
| `--on <host>` | Run it on this host, its name or ID (kantel hosts list shows them) |
| `--host-label <k=v>` | Run it only on a host with this label; repeat for more |
| `--auto-upgrade` | An isolate that becomes a microVM by itself when a command needs one, and runs it again |
| `--no-wait` | Answer at once rather than once it runs |

```sh
# A microVM: a full Linux with root, Docker and SSH
kantel new --type microvm

# A bigger one, with a name, that stops after 30 minutes unused
kantel new --type microvm --vcpus 8 --memory 16 --name ci --idle-stop 30

# One from a saved snapshot, keeping only its ID for a script
id=$(kantel new --from monorepo-ci --json | jq -r .id)

# One with two environments, where npm wins over backend
kantel new --env backend --env npm
```

### kantel sizes

The sizes and shapes a new microVM may be, from the hosts it may use.

```sh
kantel sizes [flags]
```

Each deployment's hosts decide which named sizes there are and what each holds, and may offer fewer than small, default, large and xlarge. kantel new --size takes one of these; --vcpus and --memory any other shape in the ranges shown.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--on <host>` | Only what this host offers, its name or ID |

### kantel list

List running sandboxes, or all of them.

```sh
kantel list [flags]
```

Also: `kantel ls`, `kantel sandbox list`, `kantel sandbox ls`.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--all` | Include stopped, paused and errored ones |
| `--label <k=v>` | Only those with this label (repeatable) |
| `--on <host>` | Only those on this host, its name or ID |
| `--mine` | Only your own, not the ones others share in an organisation |
| `--every-account` | In each of your accounts, with an ACCOUNT column (a personal token's) |
| `--cursor <cursor>` | The next page, from a list's More |

```sh
# The running ones
kantel list

# Every one of yours, stopped ones too, in all your accounts
kantel list --all --mine --every-account

# Those with a label, as JSON
kantel list --label team=web --json
```

### kantel info

Show a sandbox.

```sh
kantel info <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel get`, `kantel sandbox get`, `kantel sandbox info`.

### kantel start

Boot a stopped sandbox fresh from its newest snapshot.

```sh
kantel start <id> [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--no-wait` | Answer at once rather than once it runs |
| `--size <size>` | A microVM's named size, such as small, default or large (kantel sizes lists the hosts') |

### kantel stop

Stop a sandbox, keeping its disk; it then costs nothing to run.

```sh
kantel stop <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel sandbox stop`.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pause` | Pause instead, keeping its memory too (microVMs only) |
| `--wait` | Answer once it has stopped |

```sh
# Stop it, keeping its disk
kantel stop sbx_4kq9x2mt

# Pause a microVM, keeping its memory too
kantel stop sbx_4kq9x2mt --pause
```

### kantel resume

Carry on a paused or stopped sandbox, with the same ID.

```sh
kantel resume <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel sandbox resume`.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--no-wait` | Answer at once rather than once it runs |
| `--size <size>` | A microVM's named size, such as small, default or large (kantel sizes lists the hosts') |

### kantel recover

Restart the machine of a sandbox that is stuck or in error.

```sh
kantel recover <id> [flags]
```

### kantel upgrade

Turn an isolate into a microVM, with the same ID, files and settings.

```sh
kantel upgrade <id> [flags]
```

Upgrade when a command says it needs a microVM, or before work an isolate can't do: git, npm or pip packages, a build, a server, Docker. The sandbox keeps its ID, name, labels, env, environments, grants and protected variables. Its /workspace files are in the microVM at /home/user/workspace, and /workspace links there, so its paths still work. A stopped isolate comes back as a running microVM. If the microVM can't be made, the isolate is left as it was. Commands sent meanwhile wait for it.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--size <size>` | A microVM's named size, such as small, default or large (kantel sizes lists the hosts') |
| `--vcpus <n>` | The microVM's vCPUs, in place of --size; with --memory |
| `--memory <GB>` | The microVM's memory in GB, in place of --size; with --vcpus |
| `--disk <GB>` | The microVM's disk in GB (default: its size's) |
| `--image <image>` | The microVM's base image |
| `--wait` | Answer once the microVM runs (the default) |
| `--no-wait` | Answer at once rather than once it runs |

```sh
# Make an isolate a microVM of the default size
kantel upgrade sbx_4kq9x2mt

# A bigger one
kantel upgrade sbx_4kq9x2mt --vcpus 8 --memory 16
```

### kantel fork

Copy a sandbox into new ones.

```sh
kantel fork <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel sandbox fork`.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--count <n>` | How many copies (default 1) |
| `--name <name>` | The copies' name |
| `--snapshot <id>` | Copy this snapshot of it; default its newest |
| `--no-wait` | Answer at once rather than once it runs |

```sh
# Three copies of a sandbox as it is now
kantel fork sbx_4kq9x2mt --count 3
```

### kantel delete

Delete a sandbox for good (needs --yes).

```sh
kantel delete <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel rm`, `kantel sandbox delete`, `kantel sandbox rm`.

It erases the sandbox and its automatic snapshots; saved snapshots of it stay.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `-y, --yes` | Yes, delete it: this can't be undone |

```sh
# Delete a sandbox for good
kantel delete sbx_4kq9x2mt --yes
```

### kantel extend

Move a sandbox's auto-stop to this many minutes from now, or change its idle stop.

```sh
kantel extend <id> [minutes] [flags]
```

Also: `kantel sandbox extend`.

kantel extend &lt;id&gt; 120 moves its stop to two hours from now. kantel extend &lt;id&gt; --idle-stop 30 stops it once it goes 30 minutes unused, counting from now; --idle-stop never turns that off. Both may be given.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--idle-stop <minutes\|never>` | Also stop once it goes this long unused: no command, SSH, desktop, browser or port traffic |

### kantel usage

A sandbox's running time, CPU and cost over the last day, and its peak memory and CPU.

```sh
kantel usage <id> [flags]
```

Also: `kantel sandbox usage`.

The peaks are its highest single readings since it was made, kept after the readings themselves are gone and after it is deleted: size a sandbox from them, as a mean can be half its peak or less.

## Commands and files

### kantel exec

Run a command in a sandbox, with its output and exit code.

```sh
kantel exec <id> [command…] -- <command…> [flags]
```

One word is a shell command line: kantel exec &lt;id&gt; 'make &amp;&amp; make test'. Several are a command and its arguments, quoted for the shell; put them after -- when they have flags of their own: kantel exec &lt;id&gt; -- ls -la. Its stdout and stderr come out on ours, and kantel exits with its exit code (124 when it timed out). Its output comes as it is written, and kantel follows it on through a reconnect; if it can't reach Kantel for two minutes it prints the command's ID and how to attach. A server or a long job: --detach, then kantel attach &lt;id&gt; &lt;command&gt;.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--cwd <dir>` | Run it here (default the sandbox user's home) |
| `--env <K=V>` | An environment variable; repeat it |
| `--timeout <seconds>` | Kill it after this long (default 30, at most 600); 0: no limit, following its output |
| `-d, --detach` | Start it and print its ID at once, with no time limit unless --timeout gives one |
| `--attach <command>` | Follow a detached command's output to its end |
| `--status <command>` | Show a command: its state and output so far |
| `--kill <command>` | Stop a detached command |
| `--stdin` | Send this terminal's stdin to the command |

```sh
# Run a shell command line
kantel exec sbx_4kq9x2mt 'cd my-app && npm test'

# A command with flags of its own, after --
kantel exec sbx_4kq9x2mt --cwd my-app -- npm run lint -- --fix

# A dev server, left running; attach follows it
kantel exec sbx_4kq9x2mt -d -- npm run dev

# A long build with no time limit, following its output
kantel exec sbx_4kq9x2mt --timeout 0 -- make -j8
```

### kantel attach

Follow a detached command's output until it ends, and exit with its code.

```sh
kantel attach <id> <command> [flags]
```

Ctrl-C stops following; the command carries on. Its output from the start is printed first.

### kantel ps

A sandbox's commands, newest first, running ones included.

```sh
kantel ps <id> [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--cursor <cursor>` | The next page, from a list's More |

### kantel kill

Stop a running command, and everything it started.

```sh
kantel kill <id> <command> [flags]
```

### kantel files ls

List a directory in a sandbox.

```sh
kantel files ls <id> [path] [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--cursor <cursor>` | The next page, from a list's More |

### kantel files cat

Print a file from a sandbox.

```sh
kantel files cat <id> <path> [flags]
```

### kantel files put

Copy a local file (up to 1 MiB) into a sandbox.

```sh
kantel files put <id> <local> <remote> [flags]
```

A local path of - reads stdin. A binary file is sent as base64; an executable keeps its mode.

### kantel files get

Copy a file out of a sandbox.

```sh
kantel files get <id> <remote> [local] [flags]
```

The local path defaults to the file's name here; - writes it to stdout.

```sh
# Print a file
kantel files get sbx_4kq9x2mt /home/user/app/out.log -

# Copy one here
kantel files get sbx_4kq9x2mt /home/user/app/report.json
```

### kantel files rm

Delete a file, or a directory and everything in it.

```sh
kantel files rm <id> <path> [flags]
```

### kantel scp

Copy files to or from a sandbox: &lt;id&gt;:&lt;path&gt; names a path in it.

```sh
kantel scp <from> <to> [flags]
```

```sh
kantel scp ./report.txt sbx_123:/home/user/      upload a file into a directory
kantel scp sbx_123:out.zip .                      download one (relative paths are under a microVM's /home/user, an isolate's /workspace)
kantel scp -r ./site sbx_123:/srv/site            upload a directory
```

It goes through Kantel's files API, so it works on isolates too. A file over 1 MiB comes down in parts; one going up goes in parts that a command joins, which needs a microVM.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `-r, --recursive` | Copy a directory and everything in it |

```sh
# A file into a sandbox
kantel scp ./data.csv sbx_4kq9x2mt:/home/user/

# A directory out of one
kantel scp -r sbx_4kq9x2mt:/home/user/app/dist ./dist
```

### kantel push

Copy a local directory into a sandbox (in git, the files git would commit).

```sh
kantel push <id> [dir] [flags]
```

In a git repository it sends the files git tracks and the new ones .gitignore doesn't leave out, so node_modules, build output and .git stay here. Elsewhere it sends everything but .git. Into a microVM it goes as one gzipped tar that the microVM's tar extracts; into an isolate, file by file. Files already there are replaced; files you deleted here stay there. Executable bits are kept. It leaves out, at any depth, .ssh, .gnupg, .aws, .azure, .kube, .netrc, .pypirc and .docker/config.json, and, unless git tracks them, .claude, .codex, .cursor, .npmrc and .env files (not .env.example), naming each on stderr; --no-default-excludes sends them. Links to outside the directory stay here. It refuses your home directory, or a directory holding it or Kantel's config, without --allow-home, and a directory inside one it leaves out, such as ~/.ssh, without --no-default-excludes.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--to <path>` | Where in the sandbox (default &lt;dir name&gt;, under a microVM's /home/user or an isolate's /workspace) |
| `--allow-home` | Push your home directory, or one holding it, leaving Kantel's config out |
| `--no-default-excludes` | Send credentials, agents' sign-ins and .env files too |

```sh
# This repository's files (what git would commit), to /home/user/<its name>
kantel push sbx_4kq9x2mt .

# Somewhere else in the sandbox
kantel push sbx_4kq9x2mt ./web --to /srv/web
```

### kantel sync

Bring a git checkout in a microVM to this working tree, sending only a patch (--git).

```sh
kantel sync <id> [dir] [flags]
```

For a sandbox that already has a clone of this repository, such as one made from a snapshot with its dependencies installed: only the difference from the clone's base commit goes over, where kantel push sends every file. The base is --base, else the checkout's .kantel-base-sha, else the git.base label on the snapshot the sandbox was made from, else the checkout's HEAD; your repository must have it too. Here, in a copy of your index (yours isn't touched), it stages your tracked changes and the new files .gitignore doesn't leave out, and diffs that tree against the base, binary files and all. There, it runs git clean -fd, which keeps ignored files such as node_modules, and git reset --hard &lt;base&gt;, applies the patch with git apply --index and checks that git write-tree names the same tree on both sides. Anything else in the checkout (commits, changes, new files) is lost. A changed or new file push would leave out (credentials; untracked .claude, .codex, .cursor, .npmrc and .env files) stays at the base's version, named on stderr; --no-default-excludes sends it. It refuses a repository as push refuses a directory (in Kantel's config, in .ssh and the like, or your home without --allow-home), and never sends Kantel's config. The whole repository goes, whichever of its directories you name. Submodules' and Git LFS files' contents don't.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--git` | As a git patch against the checkout's base commit (the one way sync works) |
| `--to <path>` | The checkout in the sandbox (default /home/user/&lt;repository's directory name&gt;) |
| `--base <commit>` | Diff against this commit, not the one the sandbox records |
| `--allow-home` | Sync a repository that is your home directory, or holds it, leaving Kantel's config out |
| `--no-default-excludes` | Send changed credentials, agents' sign-ins and .env files too |

```sh
# Bring the sandbox's clone to this working tree, sending only a patch
kantel sync sbx_4kq9x2mt --git
```

## Ports, SSH, desktop and browser

### kantel host

Give a port in a sandbox an HTTPS URL, and print it.

```sh
kantel host <id> <port> [flags]
```

The URL carries a token unless --public: anyone holding the whole URL can open it. Asking again for the same port gives the same URL. Start the server first, with kantel exec &lt;id&gt; --detach -- &lt;command&gt;. kantel port list shows a sandbox's ports, and kantel port hide &lt;id&gt; &lt;port&gt; stops one working.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--public` | Anyone with the URL may open it, with no token |

```sh
# A private HTTPS URL for port 3000 (it carries a token)
kantel host sbx_4kq9x2mt 3000

# One anyone may open
kantel host sbx_4kq9x2mt 8080 --public
```

### kantel port list

A sandbox's exposed ports.

```sh
kantel port list <id> [flags]
```

### kantel port hide

Stop a port's URL working.

```sh
kantel port hide <id> <port> [flags]
```

### kantel ssh

A shell in a sandbox: SSH into a microVM, a pseudo-shell in an isolate; or run one command.

```sh
kantel ssh <id> [-- <command…>] [flags]
```

Connects in this terminal, through the control plane's relay when the sandbox is on its own hosts. After --, a command runs there instead of a shell, and kantel exits with its exit code: kantel ssh &lt;id&gt; -- uname -a. --print (or --json) prints the ssh command with its key and options, for scp, rsync or an ssh config entry. An isolate has no SSH: there it is a pseudo-shell over the commands API, each line one command, keeping the directory and exported variables. When a command needs a microVM it is run again there (autoUpgrade), or you're asked whether to upgrade, and then it switches to SSH on the microVM. Lines piped in run in order.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--print` | Print the ssh command that connects, rather than running it |
| `--public-key <file>` | Let in this OpenSSH public key (default: a key pair Kantel makes, kept here) |
| `--ttl <minutes>` | How long a connection can be started (default 10, at most 60) |

```sh
# A shell
kantel ssh sbx_4kq9x2mt

# One command
kantel ssh sbx_4kq9x2mt -- docker ps

# The ssh command, for an editor's remote setup
kantel ssh sbx_4kq9x2mt --print

# Lines piped to an isolate's pseudo-shell
printf 'cd app\nnode test.js\n' | kantel ssh sbx_4kq9x2mt
```

### kantel desktop

Open a microVM's desktop in your browser, and print its URL.

```sh
kantel desktop <id> [flags]
```

The URL carries a short-lived token: treat it as a secret.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--view-only` | Watch only: no keyboard or mouse |
| `--ttl <minutes>` | How long the URL can be opened for (default 10, at most 60) |
| `--print` | Print the URL without opening it |

### kantel browser

Start a microVM's Chromium: open its live view, and print that URL and its CDP URL.

```sh
kantel browser <id> [flags]
```

Drive it with Playwright: chromium.connectOverCDP(&lt;cdp URL&gt;). Both URLs carry short-lived tokens.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--view-only` | Watch only: no keyboard or mouse |
| `--ttl <minutes>` | How long the URL can be opened for (default 10, at most 60) |
| `--print` | Print the URL without opening it |

## Snapshots

### kantel snapshot list

Saved snapshots, or one sandbox's history.

```sh
kantel snapshot list [sandboxId] [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--sandbox <id>` | Only this sandbox's snapshots |
| `--saved` | Only saved snapshots |
| `--cursor <cursor>` | The next page, from a list's More |

### kantel snapshot info

A snapshot's details: what it holds, its labels, and when it was taken and saved.

```sh
kantel snapshot info <snapshot> [flags]
```

Give a snapshot's ID, or a saved snapshot's name.

### kantel snapshot take

Add a snapshot of a sandbox's disk to its history now.

```sh
kantel snapshot take <id> [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--description <text>` | What it holds |
| `--label <k=v>` | A label, such as git.base=&lt;commit&gt;; repeat for more |
| `--memory` | Keep a running microVM's memory too, so a sandbox made from it carries on where it was, on the same size only; default the disk alone |

### kantel snapshot save

Keep a sandbox's state under a name, to start new sandboxes from.

```sh
kantel snapshot save <sandboxId> <name> [flags]
```

--min-memory makes Kantel refuse a sandbox made from it with less memory, before it starts one that would run out part of the way through: kantel snapshot save &lt;id&gt; monorepo-checks --min-memory 16, then kantel new --from monorepo-checks --vcpus 8 --memory 16.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--replace` | Replace a saved snapshot of the same name |
| `--description <text>` | What it holds |
| `--label <k=v>` | A label, such as git.base=&lt;commit&gt;; repeat for more |
| `--snapshot <id>` | Save this snapshot of its history; default now |
| `--memory` | Keep a running microVM's memory too, so a sandbox made from it carries on where it was, on the same size only; default the disk alone |
| `--min-memory <GB>` | The least memory a sandbox made from it may have, such as 16 (0: none; a replace keeps its own) |

```sh
# Keep a sandbox's disk under a name, to start others from
kantel snapshot save sbx_4kq9x2mt monorepo-ci --label git.base=$(git rev-parse HEAD)

# Replace it after installing more
kantel snapshot save sbx_4kq9x2mt monorepo-ci --replace
```

### kantel snapshot files

List a directory in a snapshot.

```sh
kantel snapshot files <snapshotId> [path] [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--cursor <cursor>` | The next page, from a list's More |

### kantel snapshot rm

Delete a snapshot.

```sh
kantel snapshot rm <snapshotId> [flags]
```

## Environments and egress

### kantel env list

The account's environments, or a sandbox's in order.

```sh
kantel env list [flags]
```

A sandbox's environments are in order: where two set the same variable, secret file or repo path, the later one wins, and the sandbox's own variables (kantel new -e K=V) win over them all. Their grants add up. In the table of them, SHADOWED is what of an environment a later one sets instead, PENDING says its secret files and repos are set up when the sandbox next runs, and POSITION is what kantel env attach --position takes.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--sandbox <sandbox>` | A sandbox's environments instead, in order: what each loses to a later one, and what is pending |

```sh
# The account's environments
kantel env list

# A sandbox's, in order
kantel env ls --sandbox sbx_4kq9x2mt
```

### kantel env create

Make an environment: variables, secret files, repos and grants for new sandboxes.

```sh
kantel env create <name> [flags]
```

A name is lower-case letters, digits and hyphens, unique in the account.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--description <text>` | What it is for |

### kantel env show

Show an environment: its variables (never a protected one's value), files, repos and grants.

```sh
kantel env show <env> [flags]
```

### kantel env delete

Delete an environment, with its sealed values and files.

```sh
kantel env delete <env> [flags]
```

### kantel env attach

Add an environment to a sandbox that exists, last unless --position says otherwise.

```sh
kantel env attach <sandbox> <env> [flags]
```

Its variables, protected variables and grants apply at once: new commands see them, and on a host that supports it so do new shells, while running processes keep what they started with. A running sandbox gets its secret files and repos now, a stopped one when it next runs. Attaching one the sandbox has already moves it to --position. A sandbox has at most 10. An API key needs the exec scope.

A sandbox's environments are in order: where two set the same variable, secret file or repo path, the later one wins, and the sandbox's own variables (kantel new -e K=V) win over them all. Their grants add up. In the table of them, SHADOWED is what of an environment a later one sets instead, PENDING says its secret files and repos are set up when the sandbox next runs, and POSITION is what kantel env attach --position takes.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--position <n>` | Where it goes: 0 is first, so every other one wins over it (default last, so it wins) |

```sh
# Add npm last, so it wins over the others
kantel env attach sbx_4kq9x2mt npm

# Add backend first, so the others win over it
kantel env attach sbx_4kq9x2mt backend --position 0
```

### kantel env detach

Take an environment off a sandbox.

```sh
kantel env detach <sandbox> <env> [flags]
```

Its variables are worked out again without it, its protected variables stop resolving at once and its grants go. The secret files it wrote and the repos it cloned stay in the sandbox. An API key needs the exec scope.

```sh
# Take npm off a sandbox
kantel env detach sbx_4kq9x2mt npm
```

### kantel env set

Set a variable: plain, or protected so sandboxes get a placeholder and never the value.

```sh
kantel env set <env> <NAME>[=<value>] [flags]
```

A protected variable's value never enters a sandbox. Each sandbox gets a kph_… placeholder in its place, which the host's egress proxy swaps for the value only in requests to a --bind destination: &lt;host&gt;[/path-prefix][:METHOD,…], such as api.github.com or api.openai.com/v1/:POST,GET.

--value-stdin reads the value from stdin, which keeps it out of your shell history and the process list:

```sh
printf %s "$GH_TOKEN" | kantel env set work GH_TOKEN --value-stdin --protected --bind api.github.com
```

Setting a protected variable again with a new value rotates it: running sandboxes keep their placeholder and send the new value from their next request. It stays protected unless you give --plain. --keep-value with --bind changes where it may go without entering it again.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--env <env>` | The environment, instead of the first argument |
| `--protected` | Keep the value out of sandboxes: each gets a kph_… placeholder instead |
| `--bind <host>[/path][:METHOD,…]` | Where a protected value may be sent; repeat it |
| `--value-stdin` | Read the value from stdin, which keeps it out of your shell history |
| `--keep-value` | Change a protected variable's --bind without entering its value again |
| `--plain` | Make a protected variable plain: sandboxes then get its value |

```sh
# A plain variable
kantel env set web NODE_ENV=production

# A protected one, sent only to its API and never into a sandbox
printf %s "$TOKEN" | kantel env set web GITHUB_TOKEN --protected --bind api.github.com --value-stdin
```

### kantel env unset

Remove a variable from an environment.

```sh
kantel env unset <env> <NAME> [flags]
```

### kantel env file

Add or replace a secret file, written into each new sandbox once it runs.

```sh
kantel env file <env> <path> [flags]
```

&lt;path&gt; is where it goes in the sandbox. Its content is sealed at rest and never shown again: kantel env show lists its path, mode and size. A secret file is in the sandbox, so anything there can read it.

```sh
kantel env file work /home/user/.npmrc --from ~/.npmrc
```

kantel env file rm &lt;env&gt; &lt;path&gt; removes one.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--mode <octal>` | Its mode in the sandbox (default 0600) |
| `--from <file>` | Read it from this local file; default stdin |

### kantel env file rm

Remove a secret file from an environment.

```sh
kantel env file rm <env> <path> [flags]
```

### kantel env repo add

Clone a git repository into each new sandbox once it runs.

```sh
kantel env repo add <env> <url> [flags]
```

The URL is https://. It is cloned through the egress proxy, after the secret files are written, and a failed clone is an event on the sandbox, not an error. Adding a URL again replaces its --path and --ref.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--path <dir>` | Where in the sandbox to clone it |
| `--ref <ref>` | The branch or tag (default the repository's default) |

### kantel env repo rm

Stop cloning a repository into new sandboxes.

```sh
kantel env repo rm <env> <url> [flags]
```

### kantel env grant

Allow or refuse requests to a host, by method and path, for every sandbox made from it.

```sh
kantel env grant <env> <allow|deny> <host> [flags]
```

Grants apply on top of the account's proxy settings: the environment's, then the sandbox's own, and deny wins. A grant with --method or --path has the egress proxy open that host's HTTPS to read each request. Quote a pattern so your shell leaves its * alone:

```sh
kantel env grant work deny api.github.com --method DELETE --path '/repos/**'
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--method <METHOD>` | Only requests with this method, such as DELETE; repeat it |
| `--path <pattern>` | Only these paths: * is one segment, ** the rest; repeat it |

### kantel env grant rm

Remove one of an environment's grants.

```sh
kantel env grant rm <env> <grant-id> [flags]
```

### kantel egress

A sandbox's outbound requests: allowed or refused, and which protected variables were swapped in.

```sh
kantel egress <sandbox> [flags]
```

CODE/RULE is the X-Kantel-Proxy-Error code the sandbox saw, and the grant or setting that decided. Paths are kept without their query. An HTTPS tunnel the proxy doesn't open shows as one CONNECT, with no status: an HTTP error inside it (a 503, say) is the site's. The proxy's own failures show as upstream-failed.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--denied` | Only the refused requests |
| `--limit <n>` | At most this many, newest first (Kantel keeps 1000) |

### kantel grant

Allow or refuse one sandbox's requests to a host, by method and path.

```sh
kantel grant <sandbox> <allow|deny> <host> [flags]
```

Grants apply on top of the account's proxy settings: the environment's, then the sandbox's own, and deny wins. A grant with --method or --path has the egress proxy open that host's HTTPS to read each request. Quote a pattern so your shell leaves its * alone:

```sh
kantel grant sbx_123 deny api.github.com --method DELETE --path '/repos/**'
```

A running sandbox picks it up within seconds. kantel egress &lt;sandbox&gt; shows its grants.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--method <METHOD>` | Only requests with this method, such as DELETE; repeat it |
| `--path <pattern>` | Only these paths: * is one segment, ** the rest; repeat it |

### kantel grant rm

Remove one of a sandbox's own grants.

```sh
kantel grant rm <sandbox> <grant-id> [flags]
```

## API keys and personal tokens

### kantel key list

The account's API keys.

```sh
kantel key list [flags]
```

### kantel key create

Make a scoped API key; its secret is shown once.

```sh
kantel key create <name> [flags]
```

Scopes: sandboxes:read, sandboxes:write, sandboxes:delete, exec, files, access, snapshots:read, snapshots:write, account:read, account:admin, hosts:admin. A coding agent's key: kantel key create agent --preset agent

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--preset <agent\|ci\|read-only\|admin>` | A named set of scopes |
| `--scope <scope>` | A scope; repeat for more |
| `--expires-days <n>` | It stops working after this many days |
| `--sandbox <id>` | Limit it to this sandbox (repeatable) |

```sh
# A key for a coding agent: it makes and drives sandboxes, but can't delete them
kantel key create agent --preset agent

# A CI key that lasts 90 days
kantel key create ci --preset ci --expires-days 90
```

### kantel key rotate

Replace a key's secret; the old one stops working at once.

```sh
kantel key rotate <id> [flags]
```

### kantel key revoke

Stop a key working.

```sh
kantel key revoke <id> [flags]
```

### kantel token list

Your personal access tokens, in every account.

```sh
kantel token list [flags]
```

### kantel token create

Make a personal access token for a script; its secret is shown once.

```sh
kantel token create <name> [flags]
```

A personal token acts as you, in every account you belong to (or the --only ones), with your role there. --preset and --scope cap what it may do beyond that. It lasts 90 days unless --expires-days says, at most 366. For an agent or CI that works in one account, an API key (kantel key create) is usually better: it acts only there, with only its scopes. Scopes: sandboxes:read, sandboxes:write, sandboxes:delete, exec, files, access, snapshots:read, snapshots:write, account:read, account:admin.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--preset <agent\|ci\|read-only\|admin>` | Cap it at a set of scopes |
| `--scope <scope>` | Cap it at a scope; repeat for more |
| `--only <account>` | Only this account, by ID or name; repeat for more (default all yours) |
| `--expires-days <n>` | It stops working after this many days (90) |

### kantel token revoke

Stop one of your personal tokens working.

```sh
kantel token revoke <id> [flags]
```

## Your own hosts (experimental)

### kantel hosts add

Add a Linux machine of your own: only your account's sandboxes will run on it.

```sh
kantel hosts add [name] [flags]
```

It prints a one-line command to run on the machine, as root. kantel-host installs, dials out to Kantel and keeps that connection open: the machine needs no inbound port and may sit behind NAT. The host joins the account you act in (your personal account, or --account &lt;org&gt;); from then on that account's new sandboxes go on its own hosts, and no other account's ever do. The deployment must have account hosts turned on (KANTEL_ACCOUNT_HOSTS=experimental).

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--label <K=V>` | A label for the host; repeat it |
| `--pool <pool>` | The pool it joins, an ID or name; default the account's default pool |
| `--expires <minutes>` | How long the token lasts, 5 to 10080; default 60 |

### kantel hosts list

The hosts added to your account.

```sh
kantel hosts list [flags]
```

### kantel hosts info

One of your hosts.

```sh
kantel hosts info <id> [flags]
```

### kantel hosts drain

Stop placing new sandboxes on one of your hosts (--off to take them again).

```sh
kantel hosts drain <id> [flags]
```

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--off` | Take new sandboxes again |

### kantel hosts move

Move one of your hosts to another of your pools: it drains, and moves once it has no sandboxes.

```sh
kantel hosts move <id> <pool> [flags]
```

It takes no new sandboxes from now on, and joins the pool once its last sandbox is deleted; then it takes new sandboxes again. Moving it to the pool it is in cancels a move, leaving it draining.

### kantel hosts rm

Remove one of your hosts: revoke its credential and close its connection (needs --yes).

```sh
kantel hosts rm <id> [flags]
```

Its sandboxes keep their disks on the machine but can't be reached. To take kantel-host off the machine too, run on it: sudo kantel-host uninstall

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `-y, --yes` | Yes, remove it: it can't join again |

### kantel pools list

Your account's pools: sets of its hosts, each host in one.

```sh
kantel pools list [flags]
```

A sandbox goes on a host of a pool, and a host joins the default pool unless its token names another.

### kantel pools add

Make an empty pool in your account.

```sh
kantel pools add <name> [flags]
```

Put hosts in it with kantel hosts add --pool &lt;name&gt;, or kantel hosts move &lt;id&gt; &lt;name&gt;.

### kantel pools rename

Rename one of your pools.

```sh
kantel pools rename <pool> <name> [flags]
```

### kantel pools default

Make one of your pools the default: where hosts join and sandboxes go, naming none.

```sh
kantel pools default <pool> [flags]
```

### kantel pools rm

Delete one of your pools: an empty one that isn't the default.

```sh
kantel pools rm <pool> [flags]
```

## Coding agents

### kantel init

Teach this project's coding agents to use Kantel: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md and a kantel skill.

```sh
kantel init [flags]
```

It writes Kantel's block into AGENTS.md (Codex, pi, Cursor) and CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), replacing an older one between its markers and leaving the rest, and the kantel skill into .agents/skills (Codex, pi) and .claude/skills (Claude Code). Nothing it writes holds a key. For MCP instead: kantel agents. kantel agent setup does this and registers the MCP server too, for the agents it finds.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--global` | Install the skill for every project (~/.claude/skills, ~/.agents/skills) and skip the .md files |
| `--for <claude\|codex\|pi>` | Only for these agents; repeat it (default all three) |

```sh
# Teach this project's coding agents to use Kantel
kantel init

# For Claude Code alone, in every project
kantel init --global --for claude
```

### kantel mcp

Serve Kantel's MCP server on stdio, for a coding agent.

```sh
kantel mcp [flags]
```

Its tools create sandboxes and run commands, files, ports and snapshots in them. kantel agent setup registers it with Claude Code, Codex and Cursor.

### kantel agents

Setup for Claude Code, Codex, pi and Cursor (never with your key in it).

```sh
kantel agents [claude|codex|pi|cursor|all] [flags]
```

It prints each agent's MCP setup to copy, with the $KANTEL_API_KEY placeholder where the key goes. To have it done for you instead, for the agents on this computer: kantel agent setup.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--write` | Write the pi block into ./AGENTS.md, replacing an old one |

### kantel agent setup

Set up the coding agents on this computer to use Kantel: the skill, AGENTS.md and the MCP server.

```sh
kantel agent setup [flags]
```

It finds Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and pi by their command on your PATH or their directory in your home (~/.claude, ~/.codex, ~/.cursor, ~/.pi), and for each:

```sh
Claude Code  CLAUDE.md block, .claude/skills/kantel, claude mcp add (project scope, or user)
Codex        AGENTS.md block, .agents/skills/kantel, codex mcp add and tool_timeout_sec = 660
in ~/.codex/config.toml (Codex's MCP servers are always your own)
Cursor       AGENTS.md block, .cursor/mcp.json (or ~/.cursor/mcp.json), its other servers kept
pi           AGENTS.md block, .agents/skills/kantel (pi has no MCP: it runs kantel)
```

It sets up this project unless --global, which installs the skill under your home and registers the MCP server for every project, skipping the .md files, as kantel init --global does. Anything outside this project needs --yes, or a yes when it asks at a terminal. Run again, it changes nothing that is already set up, and says so.

Nothing it writes holds a key. The MCP server uses kantel's own sign-in (kantel login), and gets KANTEL_URL only when Kantel isn't at https://app.kantel.dev. To give an agent a scoped key of its own instead: kantel key create agent --preset agent, and set KANTEL_API_KEY where it runs.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--for <claude\|codex\|cursor\|pi>` | Only these agents; repeat it (default the ones found here) |
| `--global` | For every project: the skill under your home, and the MCP server at user scope |
| `--no-mcp` | Don't register the MCP server |
| `--no-skill` | Don't install the skill or the AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md block |
| `--dry-run` | Print every file and command it would write or run, and change nothing |
| `-y, --yes` | Yes, change files outside this project too (--global, Codex's config) |

```sh
# See what it would do for the agents found here
kantel agent setup --dry-run

# Set up this project for Claude Code and Codex
kantel agent setup --for claude --for codex --yes

# Every project, for every agent found, from a script
kantel agent setup --global --yes

# The skill and AGENTS.md block only, no MCP
kantel agent setup --no-mcp
```

## Help

### kantel help

Every command, or one command's flags and examples.

```sh
kantel help [command…] [flags]
```

With --json it prints every command, its arguments, flags and examples, and the exit codes, as JSON (or one command's, given its name): for an agent or a tool, with no sign-in and no network.

### kantel version

The version (also --version).

```sh
kantel version [flags]
```

### kantel completion

The script that completes kantel's commands, flags and sandbox IDs in bash, zsh or fish.

```sh
kantel completion <shell> [flags]
```

Prints the script that completes kantel's commands, flags and sandbox IDs in your shell. Load it:

```sh
bash: echo 'source <(kantel completion bash)' >> ~/.bashrc
zsh:  echo 'source <(kantel completion zsh)' >> ~/.zshrc
fish: kantel completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/kantel.fish
```

### kantel update

Update kantel to the latest release, or to --version.

```sh
kantel update [flags]
```

It downloads the release's kantel for this machine (kantel-&lt;os&gt;-&lt;arch&gt;), checks it against the release's SHA256SUMS and that it runs, and renames it over this one, and over kantel-admin where it is installed beside kantel. KANTEL_RELEASE_URL downloads from a mirror instead: a directory holding one release's files.

After a command, kantel says on stderr when a newer release is out, checking at most once a day. It never does with --json, when stderr isn't a terminal, in CI or under a coding agent; KANTEL_NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER=1 turns it off.

| Flag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--version <version>` | Install this release, such as 0.2.0 |
| `--check` | Only say whether there is a newer release |
| `--force` | Install it even when it is the version you have |

```sh
# Say whether there is a newer release
kantel update --check

# Update to the latest release
kantel update

# Install a release in particular
kantel update --version 0.3.2
```
